entry.sum: Division splits a number into equal parts. $12 \div 3 = 4$ can mean sharing 12 into 3 equal groups (4 in each) or making groups of 3 from 12 (4 groups). Division undoes multiplication, and when the groups do not come out exactly the leftover is a remainder, as in $28 \div 8 = 3$ R $4$.
key: a \div b = c \iff c \times b = a \quad (b \neq 0)
a = q \times b + r,\quad 0 \le r < b \quad (28 = 3 \times 8 + 4)
entry.why: Division answers every fair-sharing and equal-grouping question, and the quotient-and-remainder idea grows into fractions, divisibility and modular arithmetic.

links.note: In algebra division becomes multiplication by an inverse, and fields are number systems where every nonzero number can be divided by.
Programming languages provide integer division and a separate remainder (modulo) operation, the quotient and remainder of this page.

blocks.body:
Twelve strawberries and three friends. How can the friends share the strawberries so that it is fair? Now pack 12 cookies into bags of 4. How many bags do you fill?

Both questions are answered by division. Division splits a number into equal parts. It answers two kinds of question: how many are in each group, and how many groups there are. On this page you will learn both meanings, the words and signs we use, how division undoes multiplication, what happens with 0 and 1, what to do when there is something left over (a remainder), and how to divide bigger numbers using tens and ones.

You should already know what multiplication means and some times tables ([[multiplication]]), and how to subtract ([[addition-subtraction]]).

blocks.title: Sharing equally
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to share a number of things equally into a given number of groups and write what you did with the sign $\div$.

Try this. Take 12 counters (buttons or beans are fine) and 3 plates. Put one counter on each plate, then another on each plate, and keep going until the counters are used up. How many are on each plate?

blocks.code:
from matplotlib.patches import Circle
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.4, 2.6)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
cols = ['red', 'blue', 'green', 'purple']
for p, cx in enumerate([1.6, 4.6, 7.6]):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((cx, 1.3), 1.15, fc='white', ec='black', lw=1.5))
    for r, (dx, dy) in enumerate([(-0.42, 0.38), (0.42, 0.38), (-0.42, -0.42), (0.42, -0.42)]):
        ax.add_patch(Circle((cx + dx, 1.3 + dy), 0.3, fc='white', ec=cols[r], lw=1.6))
        ax.text(cx + dx, 1.3 + dy, str(r + 1), ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12, color=cols[r])
    ax.text(cx, -0.1, 'plate ' + 'ABC'[p] + ': 4', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlim(0.2, 9.0); ax.set_ylim(-0.45, 2.6); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 12 counters dealt onto 3 plates, one to each plate per round. The number on a counter is its round. There are 4 rounds, so each plate gets 4 counters: $12 \div 3 = 4$.
blocks.alt: Three large circles labelled plate A, plate B and plate C. Each holds four small counters numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4, one for each dealing round. Below each plate is the number 4.

blocks.title: Division as sharing
blocks.body:
When we share a number of things equally into a given number of groups and ask how many are in each group, we are dividing. Sharing 12 counters equally onto 3 plates puts 4 on each plate. We write this as

$$12 \div 3 = 4$$

and read it as twelve divided by three equals four. The sign $\div$ means divided by. The Common Core describes this meaning as finding the number of objects in each share when a number of objects is split into equal shares; IM calls it a how many in each group question.

Example: 10 pencils shared equally between 2 children gives 5 each, so $10 \div 2 = 5$.

Non-example: 12 counters put on 3 plates as 5, 4 and 3 is not division, because the shares are not equal. Division always means equal shares.

blocks.title: Finding a share by counting in the divisor
blocks.body:
To share a number equally into a given number of groups, count in steps of that size until you reach the number (this works when the number shares out exactly; remainders come later). The number of counts is the size of each share.

For 12 shared into 3 groups, count in threes: 3, 6, 9, 12. That is 4 counts, so each share is 4.

When you deal, each round puts one counter on every plate. With 3 plates, each round uses 3 counters. So after 1 round you have used 3 counters, after 2 rounds 6, after 3 rounds 9 and after 4 rounds 12. Counting in threes is counting the rounds. Every plate gets one counter in each round, so the number of rounds is the number of counters on each plate.
15 stickers are shared equally among 5 children. How many stickers does each child get?
blocks.solution:
There are 5 children, so each round of dealing uses 5 stickers.

Count in fives until you reach 15: 5, 10, 15. That is 3 counts.

So each child gets 3 stickers, and $15 \div 5 = 3$.

blocks.body: Halve 40. In other words, share 40 equally into 2 groups.
blocks.solution:
Dividing by 2 is the same as finding half.

Half of 4 tens is 2 tens, so half of 40 is 20.

So $40 \div 2 = 20$: 20 is a half of 40. Check: $20 + 20 = 40$.

items.q: 8 apples are shared equally between 2 bowls. How many in each bowl?
How do you read $18 \div 3 = 6$?
items.a: Eighteen divided by three equals six.

items.q: 9 sweets go to 3 children as 4, 4 and 1. Is that sharing equally?
items.a: No. The shares must be equal: 3 each.

items.q: To share 20 into 5 groups, which numbers do you count in?
items.a: Fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. Four counts, so 4 in each group.

items.q: 6 biscuits are shared equally between 2 friends. How many does each friend get? Write the division.
items.hint: Deal them out one each at a time, or count in twos.
items.solution: Count in twos: 2, 4, 6. That is 3 counts, so each friend gets 3. $6 \div 2 = 3$.

items.q: Share 20 marbles equally into 4 bags. How many in each bag?
items.hint: Count in fours until you reach 20.
items.solution: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 is 5 counts. Each bag has 5 marbles: $20 \div 4 = 5$.

items.q: Find half of 60. Write it as a division.
items.solution: Half of 6 tens is 3 tens, so $60 \div 2 = 30$. Check: $30 + 30 = 60$.

items.q: 35 children are split equally into 5 teams. How many children are in each team?
items.hint: Count in fives and count how many fives you say.
items.solution: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 is 7 counts. Each team has 7 children: $35 \div 5 = 7$.

items.q: Sam puts 24 cards into 3 equal piles. Then he moves 2 cards from the first pile to the second. Are the piles still equal? How many are in each pile now?
items.hint: First find the equal share. Then change two of the piles.
items.solution: Equal piles: count in threes, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 is 8 counts, so 8 in each pile ($24 \div 3 = 8$). After the move the piles hold 6, 10 and 8. They are no longer equal, so this is no longer an equal share; there are still 24 cards in all.

blocks.body:
- Sharing equally into a given number of groups is division.

- $12 \div 3 = 4$ is read twelve divided by three equals four: 3 equal groups of 4.

- The shares must be equal.

- To find a share, count in the number of groups until you reach the total.

- Dividing by 2 is halving.

blocks.title: Making equal groups
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to find how many equal groups a number makes, by repeated subtraction or by counting in the group size, and tell this meaning apart from sharing.

Try this. Put 12 counters in a pile. Take away 4 and put them in a bag. Keep taking away 4 until the pile is empty. How many bags did you fill?

blocks.code:
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyBboxPatch
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.4, 1.9)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
for g in range(3):
    x0 = 0.5 + g * 3.4
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x0 - 0.15, 0.55), 2.9, 0.9, boxstyle='round,pad=0.1', fc='white', ec='blue', lw=1.5))
    for i in range(4):
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x0 + 0.3 + i * 0.7, 1.0), 0.28, fc='black', ec='black'))
    ax.text(x0 + 1.3, 0.1, 'bag ' + str(g + 1), ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12, color='blue')
ax.set_xlim(0, 10.6); ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 1.8); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 12 cookies packed in bags of 4. Each bag holds 4 cookies and 3 bags are filled: $12 \div 4 = 3$.
blocks.alt: Twelve black dots in three rounded boxes of four dots each, labelled bag 1, bag 2 and bag 3.

blocks.title: Division as grouping
blocks.body:
When we know the size of each group and ask how many groups we can make, we are also dividing. Packing 12 cookies into bags of 4 fills 3 bags, so

$$12 \div 4 = 3.$$

OpenStax starts division with exactly this: filling bags of 4 cookies from 12. The Common Core describes this meaning as finding the number of shares when objects are split into equal shares of a given size; IM calls it a how many groups question.

Example: 20 children make teams of 5. There are 4 teams, so $20 \div 5 = 4$.

Non-example: 20 children in teams of 5, 5, 6 and 4 are not equal groups of 5, so this is not $20 \div 5$.

blocks.title: Division is repeated subtraction
blocks.body:
To find how many groups of 4 are in 12, subtract 4 again and again until nothing is left. The number of subtractions is the answer:

$$12 - 4 = 8,\quad 8 - 4 = 4,\quad 4 - 4 = 0.$$

We subtracted 3 times, so $12 \div 4 = 3$. You can also count in the group size: 4, 8, 12 is 3 counts.

Each subtraction takes away exactly one bag of 4 cookies. When the pile reaches 0, every cookie is in a bag and every bag is full. So the number of subtractions is the number of full bags. Counting 4, 8, 12 counts the cookies bag by bag, so it gives the same number. OpenStax puts it this way: multiplication is repeated addition, and division is repeated subtraction.

blocks.title: Two questions, one division
blocks.body: The same division $12 \div 4 = 3$ can be seen and described in several ways.

items.label: Grouping (quotitive)
items.body: The total and the size of each group are known; the quotient is the number of groups. 12 cookies in bags of 4 make 3 bags. NCETM calls this the quotitive structure.

items.label: Sharing (partitive)
items.body: The total and the number of groups are known; the quotient is the size of each share. 12 cookies shared among 4 friends gives 3 each. NCETM calls this the partitive structure.

items.label: How many?
items.body: IM asks two questions: how many groups? and how many in each group? The same expression, such as $6 \div 2$, can answer either: 6 blocks in stacks of 2, or 6 blocks in 2 equal stacks.

items.label: Take away again
items.body: Subtract 4 from 12 until nothing is left: three subtractions, so 3 bags.

items.label: Counters
items.body: Lay out the dividend as counters and make groups the size of the divisor. 24 counters in groups of 8 make 3 groups, so $24 \div 8 = 3$.

blocks.title: For adults: one sign, two situations
blocks.body:
Sharing and grouping look the same when written, $12 \div 4$, but they are different situations: in one, 4 is the number of groups; in the other, 4 is the size of each group. NCETM introduces both structures in Year 2 and teaches children to solve both by counting in the divisor or by using known facts.

IM has children represent and solve both kinds of problem, notice that one diagram or expression such as $6 \div 2$ can answer either question, and later interpret an expression with no story at all. With larger numbers IM lets children treat the divisor as the number of groups (as in $57 \div 3$) or as the size of each group (as in $90 \div 15$), whichever is more efficient. Its lesson on ways to divide larger numbers looks at $96 \div 8$ both ways.
A gardener has 18 seeds and puts 3 seeds in each pot. How many pots does she need? Is this sharing or grouping?
blocks.solution:
The size of each group (3 seeds) is known, and we want the number of groups. This is grouping.

Repeated subtraction: $18 - 3 = 15$, $15 - 3 = 12$, $12 - 3 = 9$, $9 - 3 = 6$, $6 - 3 = 3$, $3 - 3 = 0$. That is 6 subtractions.

Or count in threes: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 is 6 counts.

She needs 6 pots: $18 \div 3 = 6$.

blocks.body: Tell two different stories for $6 \div 2$, one of each kind.
blocks.solution:
Grouping: 6 blocks are stacked in stacks of 2. How many stacks? Answer 3, because 2, 4, 6 is 3 counts.

Sharing: 6 blocks are put into 2 equal stacks. How many in each stack? Answer 3, because dealing 6 blocks into 2 stacks takes 3 rounds.

Both stories give $6 \div 2 = 3$.

items.q: 30 eggs go into boxes of 6. Is the question how many boxes a sharing or a grouping question?
items.a: Grouping: the group size (6) is known.

items.q: Find $15 \div 5$ by repeated subtraction.
How many groups of 2 are in 10?
16 socks are put into pairs (groups of 2). How many pairs?
Find $20 \div 4$ by repeated subtraction. Show each step.
items.hint: Start at 20 and take away 4 each time until you reach 0.

items.q: Say whether each is sharing or grouping. (a) 24 chairs are put in rows of 6; how many rows? (b) 24 chairs are put in 6 equal rows; how many in each row?
items.hint: Ask: is the group size known, or the number of groups?
items.solution: (a) Grouping: the row size 6 is known; $24 \div 6 = 4$ rows. (b) Sharing: the number of rows 6 is known; $24 \div 6 = 4$ chairs in each row.

items.q: Write a grouping story and a sharing story for $14 \div 7$, and find the answer.
items.hint: In one story 7 is the size of a group; in the other, 7 is the number of groups.
items.solution: Grouping: 14 flowers in bunches of 7; there are 2 bunches. Sharing: 14 flowers shared among 7 vases; each vase gets 2. In both, $14 \div 7 = 2$ (7, 14 is 2 counts).

items.q: A rope 21 metres long is cut into pieces 3 metres long. How many pieces?
items.hint: This is grouping with lengths: how many 3s in 21?
items.solution: Count in threes: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 is 7 counts. There are 7 pieces: $21 \div 3 = 7$.

blocks.body:
- Division also answers how many equal groups: 12 cookies in bags of 4 make 3 bags.

- Division is repeated subtraction: take away the group size until nothing is left.

- Sharing (partitive) finds the size of each group; grouping (quotitive) finds the number of groups.

- Both are written the same way, $12 \div 4 = 3$.

blocks.title: Words and signs for division
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to name the parts of a division, write a division in four ways and read it aloud.

Try this. Look at $12 \div 4 = 3$. Which number was split up? Which number did the splitting? Which number is the answer?

blocks.title: Dividend, divisor and quotient
Four ways to write a division
blocks.body:
OpenStax lists four ways to write 12 divided by 4:

$$12 \div 4, \qquad 12/4, \qquad \frac{12}{4}, \qquad 4\,\overline{)\,12}$$

The third uses a fraction bar: the dividend goes on top. The fourth is the long-division layout: the dividend sits under the bracket and the divisor stands to its left. All four mean the same.

We can read $64 \div 8$ as sixty-four divided by eight, or as the quotient of sixty-four and eight.

blocks.title: Signs and names for division
blocks.body: Countries and books write and name division differently.

rows.text: Pupils write division statements with the $\div$ sign and $=$ from Year 2. The written methods are called short division and long division.
Uses $\div$, the slash $/$, the fraction bar and the long-division bracket; writes a remainder with R, as in $28 \div 8 = 3$ R $4$.

The sign $\div$ is used mainly in English-speaking countries. The standard ISO 80000-2 recommends the slash or the fraction bar for division and discourages $\div$. In Scandinavian countries $\div$ was, and sometimes still is, used as a minus sign.
NCETM (England): partitive (sharing) and quotitive (grouping). IM: how many in each group? and how many groups? Common Core: the number in each share, or the number of shares.

blocks.body: Write 35 divided by 7 in four ways and name the dividend, divisor and quotient.
blocks.solution:
The four ways: $35 \div 7$, $35/7$, $\frac{35}{7}$ and $7\,\overline{)\,35}$.

The dividend is 35 (the number divided) and the divisor is 7 (the number we divide by).

Count in sevens: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35 is 5 counts, so the quotient is 5.

items.q: In $42 \div 7 = 6$, which number is the divisor?
Write $\frac{18}{6}$ with the $\div$ sign.
In $5\,\overline{)\,45}$, which number is the dividend?
Read $72 \div 9$ aloud in two ways.
items.a: Seventy-two divided by nine; the quotient of seventy-two and nine.

items.q: Name the dividend, divisor and quotient in $30 \div 5 = 6$.
items.hint: The dividend is split up; the divisor does the splitting.
items.solution: Dividend 30, divisor 5, quotient 6.

items.q: Write $84 \div 7$ with a slash and with a fraction bar.
items.hint: The dividend comes first, or on top.

items.q: Write $6\,\overline{)\,54}$ in words, and find the quotient.
items.hint: The number under the bracket is the dividend.
items.solution: Fifty-four divided by six. Count in sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 is 9 counts, so the quotient is 9.

items.q: A German book writes $21 : 3 = 7$. Write it the English way and say what it means.
items.hint: The colon is a division sign there.
items.solution: $21 \div 3 = 7$: 21 divided by 3 is 7, because 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 is 7 counts.

items.q: The quotient is 4 and the divisor is 9. What is the dividend?
items.solution: $4 \times 9 = 36$, so the dividend is 36: $36 \div 9 = 4$.

blocks.title: Division undoes multiplication
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to use a multiplication fact to find a division, find a missing number in a division, and check a division by multiplying.

Try this. Make an array of counters: 3 rows with 4 in each row. How many counters? Now read the same array as a division in two ways.

blocks.code:
from matplotlib.patches import Circle
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.4, 2.7)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
for r in range(3):
    for c in range(4):
        ax.add_patch(Circle((0.8 + c * 0.9, 2.2 - r * 0.9), 0.3, fc='black'))
ax.text(2.15, 2.95, '4 in each row', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12)
ax.text(-0.05, 1.3, '3 rows', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12, rotation=90)
eqs = [r'$3 \times 4 = 12$', r'$4 \times 3 = 12$', r'$12 \div 3 = 4$', r'$12 \div 4 = 3$']
for i, e in enumerate(eqs):
    ax.text(5.0, 2.55 - i * 0.68, e, ha='left', va='center', fontsize=14)
ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 8.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3.25); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: An array of 12 dots: 3 rows with 4 in each row. It shows four facts: $3 \times 4 = 12$, $4 \times 3 = 12$, $12 \div 3 = 4$ and $12 \div 4 = 3$.
blocks.alt: Twelve black dots in 3 rows of 4, with labels 3 rows and 4 in each row. To the right, the equations 3 times 4 equals 12, 4 times 3 equals 12, 12 divided by 3 equals 4, and 12 divided by 4 equals 3.

blocks.title: Division is the inverse of multiplication
blocks.body:
For whole numbers, with $b$ not 0, when the division comes out exactly (no remainder; see the section Remainders),

$$a \div b = c \quad\text{means}\quad c \times b = a.$$

The letters stand for any numbers. For example, $12 \div 4 = 3$ because $3 \times 4 = 12$. So a division asks a multiplication question with a missing factor: $32 \div 8$ asks which number times 8 makes 32.

Think of grouping. Saying $a \div b = c$ means that $a$ things make exactly $c$ groups of $b$, with nothing left over. Putting the $c$ groups of $b$ back together gives $c \times b$ things, which is all $a$ of them. So $c \times b = a$.

Going the other way, if $c \times b = a$, then $c$ groups of $b$ use up all $a$ things, so $a$ makes $c$ groups of $b$, and $a \div b = c$.

blocks.title: Fact families
blocks.body:
One array gives two multiplications and two divisions. The facts $3 \times 4 = 12$, $4 \times 3 = 12$, $12 \div 3 = 4$ and $12 \div 4 = 3$ belong together. England's Year 2 notes use commutativity and inverse relations for this kind of reasoning, with $4 \times 5 = 20$ and $20 \div 5 = 4$ as the example.

Example: $6 \times 7 = 42$ gives $7 \times 6 = 42$, $42 \div 6 = 7$ and $42 \div 7 = 6$.

Non-example: $6 \times 7 = 42$ does not give $7 \div 42 = 6$. The product, 42, is always the number being divided.

blocks.title: Ways to find 32 ÷ 8
blocks.body: Sources give different routes to the same quotient.

items.label: Unknown factor
items.body: The Common Core calls this an unknown-factor problem, and IM writes $32 \div 8 = ?$ as $? \times 8 = 32$. Find the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8: $4 \times 8 = 32$, so $32 \div 8 = 4$.

items.label: Skip count
items.body: Count in eights: 8, 16, 24, 32. Four counts, so 4.

items.label: Check by multiplying
items.body: Multiply the quotient by the divisor to get back the dividend: $4 \times 8 = 32$, so the answer 4 is right.

blocks.title: For adults: move from counting to known facts
blocks.body:
Counting in eights works, but it is slow and easy to slip on. NCETM suggests moving on from skip counting to known multiplication facts (and halving facts when dividing by 2). The Common Core asks Grade 3 pupils to divide fluently within 100 using the link between multiplication and division, and England expects pupils to know the related division facts for the tables up to $12 \times 12$ by Year 4.

England's Year 2 notes link commutativity and inverse relations: from $4 \times 5 = 20$ a child also gets $20 \div 5 = 4$.
Find $54 \div 6$ using a multiplication fact, and check.
blocks.solution:
Ask: which number times 6 makes 54? Write it as $? \times 6 = 54$.

From the six times table: $9 \times 6 = 54$.

So $54 \div 6 = 9$.

Check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor: $9 \times 6 = 54$, the dividend.

blocks.body: Find the missing number: $48 \div \square = 6$.
blocks.solution:
The dividend is 48 and the quotient is 6. By the inverse rule, $6 \times \square = 48$.

From the six times table: $6 \times 8 = 48$.

So the missing number is 8. Check: $48 \div 8 = 6$, because $6 \times 8 = 48$.

blocks.body: Write the fact family for $7 \times 8 = 56$.
blocks.solution:
Swap the factors: $8 \times 7 = 56$.

Divide the product by each factor: $56 \div 7 = 8$ and $56 \div 8 = 7$.

The family is $7 \times 8 = 56$, $8 \times 7 = 56$, $56 \div 7 = 8$, $56 \div 8 = 7$.

items.q: Use $5 \times 9 = 45$ to find $45 \div 9$.
Write $27 \div 3 = ?$ as a multiplication with a missing factor.
Is $63 \div 7 = 8$ right? Check by multiplying.
items.a: No: $8 \times 7 = 56$, not 63. The answer is 9, since $9 \times 7 = 63$.

items.q: Use $4 \times 6 = 24$ to write two division facts.
items.hint: Divide the product by each factor.

items.q: Find $72 \div 8$.
Find the missing numbers: (a) $\square \div 3 = 5$; (b) $36 \div \square = 4$.
items.hint: (a) The dividend is $5 \times 3$. (b) Which number times 4 is 36?
items.solution: (a) $5 \times 3 = 15$, so $15 \div 3 = 5$; the missing number is 15. (b) $4 \times 9 = 36$, so $36 \div 9 = 4$; the missing number is 9.

items.q: Write the whole fact family for $9 \times 7 = 63$.
Find $96 \div 12$ using the twelve times table.
A class of 28 sits at tables of 4. How many tables? Write the division and the multiplication that checks it.
items.solution: $7 \times 4 = 28$, so $28 \div 4 = 7$ tables. Check: $7 \times 4 = 28$.

blocks.body:
- Division undoes multiplication: $a \div b = c$ means $c \times b = a$.

- So $32 \div 8$ asks which number times 8 makes 32.

- One array gives a fact family of two multiplications and two divisions.

- Check a division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.

- Use times-table facts rather than long counting.

blocks.title: Order matters in division
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to explain why the dividend and divisor cannot be swapped.

Try this. You know $3 \times 4 = 4 \times 3$. Is $12 \div 3$ the same as $3 \div 12$? Think of 12 cakes for 3 children, and 3 cakes for 12 children.

blocks.title: Division is not commutative
blocks.body:
Multiplication can be done in any order, but division cannot. In general $a \div b$ and $b \div a$ are different:

$$12 \div 3 = 4, \quad\text{but}\quad 3 \div 12 \neq 4.$$

(The sign $\neq$ means is not equal to.) England asks Year 2 pupils to show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order and division of one number by another cannot. One case where the order does not matter is when the two numbers are the same, as in $5 \div 5$.

One example where the swap fails is enough to show the rule is not always true. Sharing 12 cakes among 3 children gives each child 4 whole cakes. Sharing 3 cakes among 12 children cannot give anyone even 1 whole cake: there are fewer cakes than children. So $3 \div 12$ is less than 1, not 4. England's Year 4 notes use a problem of this kind: 3 cakes shared equally between 10 children.

blocks.title: Swapping the numbers
blocks.body:
NCETM's Year 4 teaching point is that multiplication is commutative but division is not. So 20 sweets shared between 4 children is $20 \div 4 = 5$; writing $4 \div 20$ would ask a different question.

The number being shared (the total) is the dividend, and it comes first.

items.q: Is $20 \div 5$ equal to $5 \div 20$?
18 pencils are shared between 3 children. Which division: $18 \div 3$ or $3 \div 18$?
Write the division for 40 stickers shared equally among 8 children, and solve it.
items.solution: $40 \div 8 = 5$, because $5 \times 8 = 40$.

items.q: Is $6 \times 2 = 2 \times 6$ true? Is $6 \div 2 = 2 \div 6$ true?
items.solution: $6 \times 2 = 12 = 2 \times 6$, true. $6 \div 2 = 3$, but $2 \div 6$ is less than 1 (2 cakes for 6 children is less than a cake each), so the second is false.

items.q: Find a pair of numbers $a$ and $b$ with $a \div b = b \div a$.
items.solution: Any two equal numbers other than 0 work, for example $a = b = 7$: $7 \div 7 = 1$ both ways.

blocks.title: Dividing with 0 and 1
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to divide by 1, divide a number by itself, divide 0, and explain why we never divide by 0.

Try this. Share 7 counters onto 1 plate. Share 7 counters onto 7 plates. Share 0 counters onto 7 plates. What is on each plate each time?

blocks.title: Rules for 0 and 1
blocks.body:
For any whole number $a$:

1. $a \div 1 = a$.

2. $a \div a = 1$, when $a$ is not 0.

3. $0 \div a = 0$, when $a$ is not 0.

4. $a \div 0$ has no answer. We say division by zero is undefined.

For example $19 \div 1 = 19$, $11 \div 11 = 1$, $0 \div 3 = 0$, and $10 \div 0$ is undefined.

Each rule follows from the inverse rule: $a \div b = c$ means $c \times b = a$.

1. $a \times 1 = a$, so $a \div 1 = a$. Sharing onto one plate puts everything on it.

2. $1 \times a = a$, so $a \div a = 1$. Sharing 7 counters onto 7 plates puts 1 on each.

3. $0 \times a = 0$, so $0 \div a = 0$. Sharing nothing gives nothing to each plate.

4. Try $10 \div 0 = c$. That would need $c \times 0 = 10$. But any number times 0 is 0, never 10, so no $c$ works. In repeated subtraction, taking away 0 again and again never makes 10 smaller, so we never finish. For $0 \div 0$, every number $c$ gives $c \times 0 = 0$, so there is no single answer either. Either way, we do not divide by 0.

blocks.title: 0 divided by a number, and a number divided by 0
blocks.body:
$0 \div 5$ and $5 \div 0$ are very different. $0 \div 5 = 0$: no sweets shared among 5 children gives each child none. $5 \div 0$ is undefined: there is no way to share 5 sweets among no children.

For adults: check the answer by multiplying. $0 \div 5 = 0$ passes, because $0 \times 5 = 0$. No answer passes for $5 \div 0$.
Find each, or say it is undefined: $14 \div 14$, $27 \div 1$, $0 \div 6$, $17 \div 0$.
blocks.solution:
$14 \div 14 = 1$, because $1 \times 14 = 14$.

$27 \div 1 = 27$, because $27 \times 1 = 27$.

$0 \div 6 = 0$, because $0 \times 6 = 0$.

$17 \div 0$ is undefined, because no number times 0 is 17.

items.q: Find $100 \div 1$ and $100 \div 100$.
items.hint: Dividing by 1 changes nothing; a number divided by itself is 1.

items.q: Find $0 \div 12$. Check by multiplying.
items.solution: $0 \div 12 = 0$. Check: $0 \times 12 = 0$.

items.q: Which of these are undefined: $0 \div 8$, $8 \div 0$, $8 \div 8$?
items.solution: Only $8 \div 0$. The others are $0 \div 8 = 0$ and $8 \div 8 = 1$.

items.q: Find the missing number: $\square \div 1 = 13$.
items.hint: Dividing by 1 gives the same number back.

items.q: Explain with a multiplication why $6 \div 0$ has no answer.
items.solution: If $6 \div 0 = c$, then $c \times 0 = 6$. But any number times 0 is 0, not 6. So there is no $c$, and $6 \div 0$ is undefined.

blocks.body:
- Order matters: $12 \div 3 = 4$, but $3 \div 12$ is less than 1.

- $a \div 1 = a$ and $a \div a = 1$ (for $a$ not 0).

- $0 \div a = 0$ (for $a$ not 0).

- Division by 0 is undefined: no number times 0 gives a number other than 0.

blocks.title: Remainders
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to divide when the numbers do not go exactly, write the remainder, and check the answer.

Try this. Pack 28 cookies into bags of 8. How many bags can you fill? How many cookies are left?

blocks.code:
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyBboxPatch
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.4, 2.9)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
for g in range(3):
    y = 2.6 - g * 0.95
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.25, y - 0.38), 6.1, 0.76, boxstyle='round,pad=0.06', fc='white', ec='blue', lw=1.5))
    for i in range(8):
        ax.add_patch(Circle((0.6 + i * 0.77, y), 0.27, fc='black'))
    ax.text(6.75, y, 'bag ' + str(g + 1), ha='left', va='center', fontsize=12, color='blue')
for i in range(4):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((0.6 + i * 0.77, -0.25), 0.27, fc='white', ec='red', lw=2.0, hatch='////'))
ax.text(3.75, -0.25, '4 left over', ha='left', va='center', fontsize=12, color='red')
ax.set_xlim(0, 8.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 3.1); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 28 cookies in bags of 8: 3 full bags hold 24 cookies, and 4 cookies are left over (striped). So $28 \div 8 = 3$ R $4$.
blocks.alt: Three rounded boxes labelled bag 1, bag 2 and bag 3, each holding a row of 8 black dots. Below them, 4 striped red circles labelled 4 left over.

blocks.title: Quotient and remainder
blocks.body:
When the dividend does not make exact groups, the amount left over is the remainder. OpenStax writes it with R:

$$28 \div 8 = 3 \text{ R } 4.$$

We read this as twenty-eight divided by eight is three remainder four. The same facts can be written with multiplication and addition:

$$28 = 3 \times 8 + 4.$$

There is no remainder when the dividend is a multiple of the divisor (a number in its times table), as $24 = 3 \times 8$. There is a remainder when it is not.

Example: $13 \div 4 = 3$ R $1$, because three groups of 4 use 12 and 1 is left.

Non-example: $28 \div 8 = 2$ R $12$ is not the answer. With 12 left you can still fill another bag of 8.

blocks.title: The remainder is less than the divisor
blocks.body:
When we divide by $b$ and make as many groups of $b$ as we can, the remainder is always less than $b$. It may be 0.

To check a division with a remainder, multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder. You must get the dividend:

$$\begin{aligned} &\text{quotient} \times \text{divisor} \\ &\quad + \text{remainder} = \text{dividend}. \end{aligned}$$

If $b$ or more things were left, we could make one more group of $b$. So when no more groups can be made, fewer than $b$ things are left.

The check works because the full groups hold quotient times divisor things, and the leftovers are the remainder. Together they are all the things we started with, the dividend.
Find $23 \div 5$ and check.
blocks.solution:
Count in fives as far as you can without passing 23: 5, 10, 15, 20. That is 4 groups, using 20.

The next count, 25, is more than 23, so stop.

Left over: $23 - 20 = 3$. Since 3 is less than 5, no more groups can be made.

So $23 \div 5 = 4$ R $3$.

Check: $4 \times 5 + 3 = 20 + 3 = 23$.

blocks.body: OpenStax gives $1439 \div 4 = 359$ R $3$. Check it.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the quotient by the divisor: $359 \times 4 = 1436$ (that is $300 \times 4 = 1200$, $50 \times 4 = 200$, $9 \times 4 = 36$, and $1200 + 200 + 36 = 1436$).

Add the remainder: $1436 + 3 = 1439$, the dividend.

The remainder 3 is less than the divisor 4. So the answer is right.

blocks.title: A remainder that is too big
blocks.body:
A slip to watch for is stopping too early, as in $38 \div 6 = 5$ R $8$. The remainder 8 is bigger than the divisor 6, so another group of 6 fits: the answer is $38 \div 6 = 6$ R $2$.

NCETM's teaching point is that the remainder is always less than the divisor, and that there is a remainder only when the dividend is not a multiple of the divisor. Comparing the remainder with the divisor is a quick way to catch this slip.

items.q: Can the remainder be 7 when you divide by 7?
items.a: No. It must be less than 7; with 7 left you can make another group.

items.q: Does $30 \div 6$ have a remainder?
Find $14 \div 3$.
items.solution: 3, 6, 9, 12 is 4 groups, using 12. $14 - 12 = 2$ is left. So $14 \div 3 = 4$ R $2$. Check: $4 \times 3 + 2 = 14$.

items.q: Find $50 \div 7$ and check.
items.solution: $7 \times 7 = 49$ and $8 \times 7 = 56$ is too big. $50 - 49 = 1$. So $50 \div 7 = 7$ R $1$. Check: $7 \times 7 + 1 = 50$.

items.q: Which of these divisions have no remainder: $35 \div 5$, $36 \div 5$, $40 \div 8$, $41 \div 8$?
items.hint: Is the dividend in the divisor's times table?
items.solution: $35 \div 5 = 7$ and $40 \div 8 = 5$ have no remainder. $36 \div 5 = 7$ R $1$ and $41 \div 8 = 5$ R $1$.

items.q: Mia says $45 \div 6 = 6$ R $9$. What is wrong? Find the right answer.
items.hint: Compare the remainder with the divisor.
items.solution: The remainder 9 is bigger than 6, so another group fits. $7 \times 6 = 42$ and $45 - 42 = 3$: $45 \div 6 = 7$ R $3$. Check: $42 + 3 = 45$.

items.q: When you divide a number by 4, which remainders are possible?
items.hint: The remainder is less than the divisor.

items.q: A number divided by 6 gives 5 R 4. What is the number?
items.hint: Use quotient times divisor plus remainder.

blocks.body:
- When the groups do not come out exactly, the leftover is the remainder: $28 \div 8 = 3$ R $4$.

- The remainder is always less than the divisor; it is 0 when the dividend is a multiple of the divisor.

- Check: quotient times divisor plus remainder equals the dividend, $3 \times 8 + 4 = 28$.

blocks.title: What does the remainder mean?
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to decide what to do with a remainder in a word problem.

Try this. 30 children go on a trip in cars that take 4 children each. $30 \div 4 = 7$ R $2$. Is the answer 7 cars? What happens to the 2 children who are left?

England asks pupils in Year 5 to interpret remainders appropriately for the context, and the Common Core asks Grade 4 pupils to solve problems in which remainders must be interpreted. The same division can need a different answer in different stories. NCETM says that in a story the answer must be interpreted carefully. By Year 6 England expects pupils to interpret remainders as whole number remainders, as fractions, or by rounding, as fits the story.

blocks.title: Three ways a remainder is used
blocks.body:
After dividing, read the question again and decide:

1. Round up, when everything must be included. 30 children, cars of 4: $30 \div 4 = 7$ R $2$, so 8 cars are needed.

2. Round down, when only full groups count. 30 centimetres of ribbon cut into pieces 4 centimetres long: $30 \div 4 = 7$ R $2$, so 7 pieces can be cut and 2 centimetres are wasted.

3. The remainder is the answer. 30 sweets shared equally among 4 children, and the rest go to the teacher: $30 \div 4 = 7$ R $2$, so the teacher gets 2.

These match England's Year 6 wording: a whole number remainder, or rounding. England's notes show that a remainder can later also be written as a fraction or a decimal: $98 \div 4$ is 24 R 2, or $24\tfrac12$, or 24.5, or about 25. Those forms belong to the pages on fractions and decimals.
A school has 50 pupils going on a trip. Each minibus holds 12 pupils. How many minibuses are needed?
blocks.solution:
Divide: $4 \times 12 = 48$ and $5 \times 12 = 60$, which is too many. So $50 \div 12 = 4$ R $2$.

Read the question again: every pupil must travel. Four minibuses take 48 pupils and leave 2 behind.

Round up: 5 minibuses are needed.

blocks.body: Eggs are sold in boxes of 6. A farmer has 40 eggs. How many full boxes can she fill?
blocks.solution:
Divide: $6 \times 6 = 36$ and $7 \times 6 = 42$, too many. So $40 \div 6 = 6$ R $4$.

Only full boxes count, so round down.

She can fill 6 full boxes, and 4 eggs are left over.

items.q: 25 people, tables for 6. $25 \div 6 = 4$ R $1$. How many tables are needed?
You have 25 dollars and books cost 6 dollars each. How many books can you buy?
items.a: 4 (you cannot buy part of a book), with 1 dollar left.

items.q: 25 stickers are shared among 6 children, and the rest are kept. How many are kept?
A minibus takes 5 people. 23 people need a lift to a match. How many minibus journeys are needed?
items.solution: $23 \div 5 = 4$ R $3$ (since $4 \times 5 = 20$). Four journeys carry 20 people and leave 3, so 5 journeys are needed.

items.q: A baker has 50 buns and packs them in bags of 8. How many full bags, and how many buns are left?
items.solution: $50 \div 8 = 6$ R $2$: 6 full bags and 2 buns left.

items.q: A tin holds 9 pencils. How many tins are needed for 75 pencils?
items.hint: Every pencil goes in a tin.
items.solution: $8 \times 9 = 72$ and $75 - 72 = 3$, so $75 \div 9 = 8$ R $3$. Round up: 9 tins.

items.q: A 70 centimetre strip of wood is cut into pieces 8 centimetres long. How many pieces, and how much is left?
items.solution: $8 \times 8 = 64$ and $9 \times 8 = 72$ is too much. $70 \div 8 = 8$ R $6$: 8 pieces and 6 centimetres left.

items.q: Write one story for $38 \div 4$ where the answer is 10, one where it is 9, and one where it is 2.
items.solution: $38 \div 4 = 9$ R $2$, since $9 \times 4 = 36$. Answer 10: 38 children, cars of 4; how many cars are needed? Answer 9: 38 tennis balls in tubes of 4; how many full tubes? Answer 2: 38 cards dealt equally to 4 players; how many are left over?

blocks.body:
- In a story, decide what the remainder means.

- Round up when everything must be included; round down when only full groups count.

- Sometimes the remainder itself is the answer.

- Later, remainders are also written as fractions or decimals.

blocks.title: Dividing bigger numbers with place value
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to divide a two-, three- or four-digit number by a one-digit number by splitting it into tens and ones (or hundreds, tens and ones).

Try this. Show 69 with base-ten blocks: 6 tens and 9 ones. Share them equally into 3 groups. Share the tens first, then the ones. What is in each group?

blocks.title: Dividing by parts
blocks.body:
To divide a big number, split it into parts that are easy to divide, divide each part, and add the answers. For $69 \div 3$:

$$\begin{aligned} 69 \div 3 &= 60 \div 3 + 9 \div 3 \\ &= 20 + 3 = 23. \end{aligned}$$

Here $60 \div 3 = 20$ comes from the fact $6 \div 3 = 2$: 6 tens shared into 3 groups is 2 tens each. In the same way England's notes derive $600 \div 3 = 200$ from $2 \times 3 = 6$. The Common Core asks Grade 4 pupils to divide numbers up to four digits by a one-digit number with strategies based on place value and the link to multiplication, shown with equations, arrays or area models. NCETM calls this partitioning.

Example: $84 \div 4 = 80 \div 4 + 4 \div 4 = 20 + 1 = 21$.

Non-example: $84 \div 4$ is not $84 \div 2 + 84 \div 2$. We split the dividend into parts, never the divisor.

blocks.title: Splitting the dividend
blocks.body:
If a number is split into two parts that both divide exactly by $b$, then the number divided by $b$ is the sum of the parts divided by $b$:

$$(p + q) \div b = p \div b + q \div b.$$

If only the first part divides exactly, the same works and the remainder of the second part is the remainder of the whole, as in $97 \div 4$ below.

This is the distributive property ([[distributive-property]]) used for division.

Share the first part, $p$, equally into $b$ groups: each group gets $p \div b$. Then share the second part, $q$, into the same $b$ groups: each group gets $q \div b$ more. Now all $p + q$ things are shared equally, and each group holds $p \div b + q \div b$. That is $(p + q) \div b$.

Check with multiplication for $69 \div 3$: $23 \times 3 = 20 \times 3 + 3 \times 3 = 60 + 9 = 69$.

blocks.caption: $45 \div 3$ with base-ten blocks. Left: 45 as 4 tens and 5 ones. Right: 3 equal groups, each with 1 ten and 5 ones, so $45 \div 3 = 15$. After 1 ten went to each group, 1 ten was left; it was exchanged for 10 ones, making 15 ones, 5 for each group.
blocks.alt: On the left, four vertical rods of ten squares and five single squares, labelled 4 tens, 5 ones. An arrow points right to three blue rounded boxes, each holding one rod of ten and five single squares, labelled 1 ten, 5 ones.

blocks.body: Find $45 \div 3$ by sharing tens and ones.
blocks.solution:
45 is 4 tens and 5 ones.

Share the 4 tens into 3 groups: 1 ten in each group uses 3 tens, and 1 ten is left.

Exchange the leftover ten for 10 ones. Now there are $10 + 5 = 15$ ones.

Share the 15 ones into 3 groups: $15 \div 3 = 5$ in each.

Each group has 1 ten and 5 ones, which is 15. So $45 \div 3 = 15$.

Check: $15 \times 3 = 30 + 15 = 45$.

blocks.code:
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.4, 2.4)
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), 6.0, 1.6, fc=(0.85, 0.9, 1.0), ec='black', lw=1.5))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((6.0, 0), 1.8, 1.6, fc=(1.0, 0.9, 0.8), ec='black', lw=1.5, hatch='//'))
ax.text(3.0, 0.8, r'$3 \times 20 = 60$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14)
ax.text(6.9, 0.8, '18', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, bbox=dict(fc='white', ec='none', pad=1))
ax.text(3.0, 1.9, '20', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=13)
ax.text(6.9, 1.9, '6', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=13)
ax.text(-0.3, 0.8, '3', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=13)
ax.text(3.9, -0.4, r'$60 + 18 = 78$, so $78 \div 3 = 20 + 6 = 26$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlim(-0.7, 8.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.8, 2.2); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: An area model for $78 \div 3$. A rectangle with area 78 and one side 3 is split into a part of area 60 (side 20) and a part of area 18 (side 6). The other side is $20 + 6 = 26$, so $78 \div 3 = 26$.
blocks.alt: A long rectangle with height labelled 3, split into a wide left part labelled 20 across the top with 3 times 20 equals 60 inside, and a narrow hatched right part labelled 6 with 18 inside. Below: 60 plus 18 equals 78, so 78 divided by 3 equals 20 plus 6 equals 26.

blocks.title: Ways to find 78 ÷ 3
blocks.body: IM, the Common Core and NCETM show different routes to the same quotient.

items.label: Tens twice
items.body: $3 \times 10 = 30$, and again $3 \times 10 = 30$, which uses 60; then $3 \times 6 = 18$ uses the rest. So the quotient is $10 + 10 + 6 = 26$.

items.label: Twenty and six
items.body: $3 \times 20 = 60$ and $3 \times 6 = 18$, and $60 + 18 = 78$, so the quotient is $20 + 6 = 26$.

items.label: Area model
items.body: Draw a rectangle of area 78 with one side 3; split it into areas 60 and 18. The other side is $20 + 6 = 26$.

items.label: Tens, exchange, ones
items.body: 7 tens shared into 3 groups is 2 tens each with 1 ten left; exchange it for 10 ones, making 18 ones, which is 6 each. Each group has 26.

blocks.body: Find $456 \div 3$.
blocks.solution:
Split 456 into parts that 3 divides exactly, working from the left. In the hundreds, 3 hundreds divide by 3 ($3 \div 3 = 1$), so take 300. That leaves $456 - 300 = 156$. In 156, take 15 tens, which is 150, because $15 \div 3 = 5$. That leaves 6. So $456 = 300 + 150 + 6$.

Divide each part: $300 \div 3 = 100$, $150 \div 3 = 50$, $6 \div 3 = 2$.

Add: $100 + 50 + 2 = 152$. So $456 \div 3 = 152$.

Check: $152 \times 3 = 300 + 150 + 6 = 456$.

blocks.body: Find $97 \div 4$.
blocks.solution:
Split off a part that 4 divides exactly: $97 = 80 + 17$.

$80 \div 4 = 20$ (since $8 \div 4 = 2$).

$17 \div 4 = 4$ R $1$ (since $4 \times 4 = 16$).

Add the quotients: $20 + 4 = 24$, and keep the remainder 1. So $97 \div 4 = 24$ R $1$.

Check: $24 \times 4 + 1 = 96 + 1 = 97$.

blocks.body: Find $2596 \div 4$ (an example from OpenStax, which finds 649).
blocks.solution:
Split 2596 into parts that 4 divides exactly, working from the left. 25 hundreds is the first part big enough to divide by 4. The biggest multiple of 4 up to 25 is 24, so take 24 hundreds, 2400. That leaves $2596 - 2400 = 196$. In 196, take 16 tens, 160 (16 is the biggest multiple of 4 up to 19). That leaves 36. So $2596 = 2400 + 160 + 36$.

$2400 \div 4 = 600$ (since $24 \div 4 = 6$).

$160 \div 4 = 40$ (since $16 \div 4 = 4$).

$36 \div 4 = 9$.

Add: $600 + 40 + 9 = 649$. So $2596 \div 4 = 649$.

Check: $649 \times 4 = 2400 + 160 + 36 = 2596$.

blocks.title: Short division and long division
blocks.body: England's notes for Years 3 and 4 lead to a compact written layout for this same idea, called short division, which is required in Year 5: the digits are divided from left to right, and a leftover is exchanged into the next column. NCETM builds it straight from partitioning. Long division, used in Year 6 and by OpenStax for bigger divisors, writes out each multiply and subtract step. These written methods have their own page (Long division).

items.q: Find $66 \div 3$ by splitting into tens and ones.
Use $8 \div 4 = 2$ to find $800 \div 4$.
For $52 \div 4$, you share 5 tens into 4 groups. How many tens are left to exchange?
items.a: 1 ten (each group gets 1 ten, using 4). Then 12 ones give 3 each: $52 \div 4 = 13$.

items.q: Find $88 \div 4$.
Find $900 \div 3$ and $350 \div 5$.
items.solution: $9 \div 3 = 3$, so $900 \div 3 = 300$. $35 \div 5 = 7$, so 35 tens divided by 5 is 7 tens: $350 \div 5 = 70$.

items.q: Find $72 \div 3$ by exchanging.
items.solution: 7 tens into 3 groups: 2 tens each, using 6 tens, 1 ten left. Exchange it: $10 + 2 = 12$ ones, so 4 ones each. Each group has 24: $72 \div 3 = 24$. Check: $24 \times 3 = 72$.

items.q: Find $84 \div 7$.
Find $635 \div 5$.
Find $79 \div 6$ and check.
A school buys 1248 pencils and shares them equally among 8 classes. How many pencils does each class get?
Find $2635 \div 7$ and check.

blocks.body:
- Split the dividend into parts that divide exactly, divide each part, and add: $69 \div 3 = 20 + 3 = 23$.

- Use place value: $6 \div 3 = 2$ gives $60 \div 3 = 20$ and $600 \div 3 = 200$.

- A leftover ten is exchanged for 10 ones; a leftover hundred for 10 tens.

- An area model shows the parts as pieces of a rectangle.

- Check by multiplying, adding any remainder.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
The written methods of short and long division do the place-value splitting digit by digit, and with them you can divide by numbers with two or more digits. The fraction bar in $\frac{12}{4}$ is a sign that division and fractions are the same idea: later, $3 \div 4$ (3 cakes shared among 4 people) becomes the fraction three quarters, and remainders can be written as fractions or decimals. Sharing a total equally is also the idea behind the mean (average) of some numbers.

The fact that the remainder is less than the divisor is the start of number theory. For whole numbers $a$ and $b$ with $b$ not 0, there is exactly one quotient $q$ and remainder $r$ with $a = q \times b + r$ and $r$ less than $b$. This is the division algorithm on the page [[divisibility]], where it leads to the Euclidean algorithm. Working only with remainders gives modular arithmetic ([[congruences]]), the arithmetic of clocks.

In algebra, division is defined as multiplying by an inverse: dividing by 4 is multiplying by one quarter. A field is a number system where every number except 0 can be divided by; a ring ([[rings]]) need not allow this, which is why whole numbers need remainders. Division by 0 stays undefined everywhere.

blocks.title: For older readers: division does not always make smaller
blocks.body: For whole numbers, dividing by a number bigger than 1 gives a smaller answer. Many learners turn this into a rule, division makes smaller, which breaks when they meet fractions and decimals: dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger answer. Lim (2011) reports that prospective teachers held this belief too, and that asking them to predict answers before calculating helped them see that the rule does not always hold.

checks.python:
# S2
assert 12 - 4 == 8 and 8 - 4 == 4 and 4 - 4 == 0 and 12 // 4 == 3
assert 20 // 5 == 4 and 5 + 5 + 6 + 4 == 20
assert 24 // 8 == 3 and 12 // 4 == 3
assert 96 % 8 == 0
x = 18; n = 0
while x: x -= 3; n += 1
assert n == 6 and list(range(3, 19, 3)) == [3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18]
assert 6 // 2 == 3 and list(range(2, 7, 2)) == [2, 4, 6]
assert 30 % 6 == 0
assert 15 - 5 == 10 and 10 - 5 == 5 and 5 - 5 == 0
assert len(range(2, 11, 2)) == 5
assert len(range(2, 17, 2)) == 8
assert [20 - 4 * k for k in range(6)] == [20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0]
assert 24 // 6 == 4 and 24 % 6 == 0
assert 14 // 7 == 2 and list(range(7, 15, 7)) == [7, 14]
assert len(range(3, 22, 3)) == 7 and 21 // 3 == 7

# S8
from fractions import Fraction as F
assert divmod(30, 4) == (7, 2)
assert divmod(98, 4) == (24, 2) and F(98, 4) == F(49, 2) == 24 + F(1, 2) and 98 / 4 == 24.5 and round(98/4 + 0.01) == 25
assert divmod(50, 12) == (4, 2) and 4 * 12 == 48 and 5 * 12 == 60
assert divmod(40, 6) == (6, 4) and 6 * 6 == 36 and 7 * 6 == 42
assert divmod(25, 6) == (4, 1)
assert divmod(23, 5) == (4, 3) and divmod(50, 8) == (6, 2) and 6 * 8 == 48
assert divmod(75, 9) == (8, 3) and 8 * 9 == 72
assert divmod(70, 8) == (8, 6) and 8 * 8 == 64 and 9 * 8 == 72
assert divmod(38, 4) == (9, 2) and 9 * 4 == 36

# figures
plates = [[1, 2, 3, 4]] * 3
assert sum(len(p) for p in plates) == 12 and all(len(p) == 4 for p in plates)
bags = [4, 4, 4]; assert sum(bags) == 12 and len(bags) == 3
assert 3 * 4 == 12
assert 3 * 8 + 4 == 28 and 3 * 8 == 24
assert 4 * 10 + 5 == 45 and 3 * (10 + 5) == 45
assert 3 * 20 == 60 and 3 * 6 == 18 and 60 + 18 == 78 and 20 + 6 == 26

# review additions
assert 456 - 300 == 156 and 156 - 150 == 6 and 456 // 3 == 152 and 3 // 3 == 1
assert 2596 - 2400 == 196 and 196 - 160 == 36 and 2500 > 2400 and 24 % 4 == 0 and 28 % 4 == 0 and 16 % 4 == 0 and 20 % 4 == 0
assert divmod(23, 5) == (4, 3) and 4 * 5 == 20
assert 20 // 4 == 5 and 20 / 4 == 5 and 4 / 20 < 1
assert 57 % 3 == 0 and 90 % 15 == 0 and 96 % 8 == 0 and 6 // 2 == 3
# split with remainder in the second part
p, q, b = 80, 17, 4
assert p % b == 0 and divmod(p + q, b) == (p // b + q // b, q % b)
# equal pairs with a == b nonzero
assert all(a / a == a / a for a in range(1, 50)) and all((a / b == b / a) == (a == b) for a in range(1, 30) for b in range(1, 30))
# exact division rule a // b == c iff c * b == a (exact case)
assert all((a % b == 0 and a // b == c) == (c * b == a) for a in range(1, 60) for b in range(1, 20) for c in range(0, 60))
assert all(0 <= a % b < b and a == (a // b) * b + a % b for a in range(0, 200) for b in range(1, 20))
